claims.claim: Dietary fiber is the part of plant foods the body cannot digest; it moves through the digestive tract mostly unchanged. NIH MedlinePlus describes fiber as a substance in plants, and the National Academy of Medicine defines dietary fibers as nondigestible carbohydrates that occur naturally in plants.
Soluble fiber dissolves in water and forms a gel during digestion, which slows digestion; well-known sources include oats, barley, beans, lentils, apples, blueberries, and nuts.

Insoluble fiber does not dissolve in water; it adds bulk to stool and helps food move through the digestive system, promoting regularity and helping prevent constipation; sources include wheat bran, whole wheat products, brown rice, quinoa, leafy greens, and many vegetables.
Fiber supports digestion and helps prevent constipation; increasing fiber too quickly can cause gas, bloating, and cramps, so it should be added gradually with adequate fluid intake.

Soluble fiber can help lower blood cholesterol (it binds bile acids, prompting the liver to pull cholesterol from the blood) and slows the rise in blood sugar after meals; higher fiber intake is associated with lower risk of heart disease, diabetes, and constipation.

Because the body cannot digest fiber, most of it is not absorbed and it contributes very little energy compared with other carbohydrates; it is not literally zero because bacteria ferment part of it in the large intestine, and fiber-rich foods still supply calories from their other components.

General guidance for daily fiber intake is about 21 to 38 grams a day for older children, adolescents, and adults, with the exact amount varying by age and sex; most people in the United States do not eat enough fiber.

Good food sources of dietary fiber include beans and lentils, oats, fruits, vegetables, and whole grains; the Dietary Guidelines for Americans (2025-2030) prioritize fiber-rich whole grains, and refining grains removes much of their fiber.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Soluble vs insoluble classification of specific foods
positions: Some guides label particular foods as 'soluble-fiber foods' and others as 'insoluble-fiber foods'
Most plant foods contain both types of fiber in varying amounts
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the two behaviors and notes that most plant foods contain both types, using each food's dominant type only for illustration, so no food is falsely classified as all one type.

positions: Fiber is not digested, so it contributes essentially no energy
Bacteria ferment part of the fiber in the large intestine, and fiber-rich foods contain calories from other components
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states fiber is mostly not absorbed and contributes very little energy, explicitly avoiding the claim that it is 'zero calorie,' and notes that fiber-rich foods still supply calories from their other parts.

positions: Precise gram targets set by age and sex group (e.g., National Academy of Medicine Adequate Intakes)
A single general band (21-38 grams per day)
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson gives the general 21-38 gram band attributed to NIH MedlinePlus and notes the exact amount varies by age and sex, framed as general guidance rather than a prescription.
